questions.q: What are the two childhood objects Bergman describes that first sparked his fascination with moving images, and what sensory details does he associate with each?
questions.a: The magic lantern (metal box, carbide lamp smell, coloured glass slides of Red Riding Hood where the wolf represented the Devil) and the rattling film projector (chimney, lamp, brown nine-foot film of a girl waking in a meadow). A wrong answer (e.g., mentioning only the projector or missing the Devil/wolf symbolism) reveals the student hasn't grasped how Bergman links *both* objects to his core themes: the lantern connects to his vicarage upbringing and personification of evil, while the projector introduces the "conjurer" metaphor central to his adult identity. Missing either breaks the developmental arc.

questions.q: Bergman writes: "A child who is born and brought up in a vicarage acquires an early familiarity with life and death behind the scenes." Explain in your own words how this upbringing shaped his artistic sensibility, using two specific textual references.
questions.a: The vicarage exposed him to rituals (funerals, marriages, baptisms) as constructed performances — "behind the scenes" — making him aware of life's theatricality. This birthed his need to "personify" the Devil via the magic lantern (transforming abstract evil into a tangible wolf slide) and later informed his view of film as "conjuring tricks" that manipulate audience emotions. A wrong answer focusing only on religious *belief* misses Bergman's explicit statement that religious emotion is "something I got rid of long ago" — his sensibility is *intellectual*, not emotional, treating existential questions as structural problems (the "tower of Babel" metaphor).

questions.q: Apply Bergman's distinction between film and literature to analyze why he calls the screenplay "an almost impossible task." Your answer must reference the "rhythm vs. intellect" contrast and the "musical score" analogy.
questions.a: Literature works through conscious intellect→imagination→emotion; film bypasses intellect to hit feelings directly via rhythm ("inhalation and exhalation"). The screenplay must translate non-verbal rhythms, moods, and "scents" into words — but written dialogue is a "musical score" requiring performance to live. Bergman squeezes location/character instructions into scripts, yet admits success depends on unpredictable "writing ability and perceptiveness." A wrong answer citing only "difficulty of writing" misses the ontological gap: he's not translating *story* but *visceral rhythm*, which words inherently flatten. This is why he says film "has nothing to do with literature."

questions.q: Compare Bergman's "cathedral of Chartres" metaphor with his description of the contemporary film industry as a "tightrope without a net." What does this contrast reveal about his character's central tension?
questions.a: The cathedral represents anonymous collective creation for a higher purpose ("glory of God"), where artists were "unknown" and "humility" was natural. The tightrope represents solitary commercial pressure where "failure, criticism, public indifference" threaten artistic survival. Bergman's character tension: he *craves* the cathedral's selfless craftsmanship ("pride of a good craftsman") but is forced into the tightrope's ego-driven marketplace. He refuses compromise ("no skill in the art of compromise"), making his integrity both his strength and his vulnerability. A wrong answer seeing only "idealism vs. realism" misses the psychological depth: his rebellion against bourgeois parents *became* his cathedral-building discipline, yet the industry demands he sell that very discipline as a commodity.

questions.q: Evaluate Bergman's claim: "I refuse to interpret my work to others... each person has the right to understand a film as he sees it." Does this stance align with or contradict his earlier admission that he "squeezes instructions as to location, characterisation and atmosphere into my screenplays"? Justify with textual evidence.
questions.a: It aligns through a crucial distinction: the *screenplay* guides collaborators (director's "marching orders" for the crew), but the *finished film* belongs to the audience. Bergman controls the "how" of production (rhythm, casting, montage) to serve his vision, then releases the "what" of interpretation. He admits reviewers have "every right to interpret my films as they like" because "a film is made to create reaction." A wrong answer calling this a contradiction misses his dual role: authoritarian craftsman during production (he must be "a devil to yourself in the screening room"), humble servant after release. This duality *is* his character — control freak as director, anarchist as artist.

questions.q: Create a 100-word "director's statement" in Bergman's voice for a hypothetical film about a watchmaker who hears time as music. Use at least three character-defining phrases/concepts from the text (e.g., "split-second impressions," "conjurer," "rhythm," "cathedral").
questions.a: *Sample:* "My film begins with a split-second impression: a gear's click sounding like a cello note. I am the conjurer, deceiving your eye with 24 frames of darkness per second so you hear time's rhythm. The watchmaker doesn't repair clocks — he conducts them. No dialogue explains this; the montage breathes it. I build my cathedral frame by frame, anonymous, not for your intellect but your pulse. If you leave humming the tick-tock, I have told the truth." A poor answer uses the phrases decoratively without integrating Bergman's core philosophy: rhythm as primary language, deception as truth-telling, anonymity as artistic goal.
